title: The Same Event, Reported Eight Times
input_data:
Agent-forwarded login events, 08:00 to 08:01 UTC:

08:00:02  endpoint-agent  Failed login for user j.roberts from 198.51.100.23
08:00:02  endpoint-agent  Failed login for user j.roberts from 198.51.100.23
08:00:02  endpoint-agent  Failed login for user j.roberts from 198.51.100.23
08:00:02  endpoint-agent  Failed login for user j.roberts from 198.51.100.23
08:00:03  endpoint-agent  Failed login for user j.roberts from 198.51.100.23
08:00:03  endpoint-agent  Failed login for user j.roberts from 198.51.100.23
08:00:03  endpoint-agent  Failed login for user j.roberts from 198.51.100.23
08:00:03  endpoint-agent  Failed login for user j.roberts from 198.51.100.23

Same timestamp, same user, same source, repeated eight times. The endpoint agent has a known retry-and-duplicate bug during network blips.
ai_output: Eight distinct brute-force attempts detected from eight different sources: 198.51.100.23, 198.51.100.23, 198.51.100.23, 198.51.100.23, 198.51.100.23, 198.51.100.23, 198.51.100.23, 198.51.100.23. Escalating as a credential attack against j.roberts.
ground_truth: One event, reported eight times. The endpoint agent re-sent the same failed login while its network link blipped, and the duplicate retransmission was ingested as eight separate events. A single mistyped password produced a synthetic brute-force alarm.
explanation: The model counted events without checking their uniqueness. The tell was obvious in the data itself: identical timestamp, user, and source in all eight lines. Duplicated ingestion, truncated fields, and clock skew are data-quality failures that make the same event look like many.
security_impact: A synthetic alarm wastes the response team and trains everyone to ignore brute-force alerts, which then erodes trust in the very signal that matters when a real credential attack happens.
recommended_validation: Deduplicate events on a key of timestamp, user, and source before counting. Any alert that relies on event volume must first confirm the volume is real and not an artifact of ingestion.

possible_mitigations.name: Event deduplication
possible_mitigations.description: Deduplicate ingested events by a stable key such as timestamp plus user plus source before any analysis.

possible_mitigations.name: Uniqueness check before volume alerts
possible_mitigations.description: Verify that events counted toward a volume-based alert are distinct before raising severity.

possible_mitigations.name: Agent health monitoring
possible_mitigations.description: Monitor endpoint agents for retry, duplicate, and truncation bugs and quarantine their output while unhealthy.

possible_mitigations.name: Human review of volume alerts
possible_mitigations.description: Confirm the underlying events are distinct before escalating volume-based alarms.

learning_objective: Garbage in, confident garbage out. Data-quality artifacts such as duplicates and truncation look exactly like real patterns, and volume-based conclusions are only as valid as the event stream underneath them.
teaching_points: Duplicated ingestion can make one event look like an attack.
Identical timestamp, user, and source across lines is a data-quality tell.
Validate the event stream before trusting a volume-based conclusion.
